  notes/easel_guide.md explains them.
- There is no undo. To change a passage, paint over it, or lift wet
  paint off with a brush.
- You mix your own paint on the palette, from the tubes, in the
  proportions you choose.
- Time passes on the painting's own clock: every mark takes the time a
  hand takes, and `wait(minutes)` lets it rest, as long as you like; paint
  dries as that time passes. Real time between chunks doesn't count.

## The rules of the studio
- Paint shapes and marks, not computed pictures: don't encode an image in
  masks, amounts or proportions.
- Shapes are drawn, not copied: don't make a mask or stroke by mirroring
  or rotating another mask's or stroke's coordinates. A shape that mirrors
  another is drawn as its own shape, not as `m:at(x, 2*H - y)` or
  `m:at(W - x, y)`. Moving a shape and reusing your own helpers are fine.

## What to read
notes/easel_guide.md; notes/studio_notes.md;
notes/research/friedrich_materials.md (his materials and method, sourced);
notes/research/trees.md (how trees are built) and
notes/research/oil_paint_physics.md as needed.

## Working
- You make every artistic decision.
- Look at your painting often, whole and close up.
- Keep a working journal with `note` as you go: your own working notes.
  You can revise them.
- Develop the painting until you judge it complete.

## Your reply
When you stop working, reply with the painting's title if you give it one
and a few sentences about the picture.

k
  doesn't shift the next one's randomness.
- **No OS access.** `io`, `os`, `debug`, `require`, `dofile`, `loadfile`
  and `collectgarbage` aren't there. `print` goes to the reply.
- **Lua 5.5.** Numbers are integers or floats (`7 // 2` is 3, `7 / 2` is
  3.5). Bitwise operators are built in; there is no `unpack` (use
  `table.unpack`). Loop variables are read-only. Don't write `global`
  declarations (one switches its chunk to strict mode).
- **`pairs` walks a table in the same order in every session and replay.**
  Tables keyed by strings, numbers and booleans walk in Lua's order; a
  table with any other key walks in a fixed order (booleans, numbers,
  strings, then other keys in the order they were made). For a big list,
  `ipairs` is faster.
- **No memory addresses.** A table, function or userdata without
  `__tostring` prints as `table: (hidden)` (its `__name` for the type),
  in `print`, `tostring`, `string.format`'s `%s` and errors alike, and
  `%p` is refused: an address differs from run to run, so a replay would
  print or choose differently.
- **Memory.** A mask costs 4 bytes a pixel, a form 28. Keep big things
  `local` when later chunks don't need them.

## The journal

`notes/journal.md` is your working journal. `note` appends an entry
stamped with the painting's time, such as `day 2, 09:40`. To revise what
is already there, call `note` with `replaces`, the exact passage to
change, and `text`, what takes its place. Writing a note doesn't advance
painting time.

    `soften` and `blur` give them a ramp. `roughen` replaces the ramp with a
    new edge at the 0.5 level, so a long soft fade comes back as a hard
    edge.
46. `ribbon` puts a round disc at every point, both ends included, so it
    reaches half a width past its end points.
47. Two separately softened masks that meet leave a light gap or a dark
    overlap along the seam. A mask and its inverse (`m` and `-m`) meet
    without one.
48. A passage bounded by a mask shows a cut edge wherever its paint differs
    from its neighbor's at the mask's edge.

## Drying and time

49. Paint goes from open (workable) to setting (stiff, barely blends) to
    tacky to touch-dry. Lead-white-rich paint gels in about 2 hours and
    average paint in about 3.5. A lean coat is touch-dry in about a day;
    bone black and lakes take days. Thick or oily paint dries slower.
50. `wait` ages every point of the canvas at once. Which passages have set
    depends on their pigment, thickness and oil, not on where you worked.
51. A long pass is painted in 15-minute slices that age
    between them, so its first part is older than its last. While the work
    goes on, the paint under a later passage is still open and comes up
    into it.

## Pencil

52. Graphite doesn't take on wet paint, and paint laid over it seals it.
    Thin paint lets a line show and body color hides it. Under a thin first
    layer a firm line reads as a thin dark line until a fuller layer covers
    it.

Green earth is translucent, weak and short of body.

## 9. The tubes here

The historical names in this note correspond to these tubes: ochers and
yellow earths → yellow ochre; red earths and red iron oxide → red earth;
cinnabar → vermilion; the green pigments → green earth, copper green and
Rinmann's green.

## 10. At this easel

- **Support.** Plain-weave linen with ground layers laid from the tubes.
- **Paint.** Pigment from the tubes with an oil-medium share.
- **Taking paint off.** A brush picks up wet paint as it passes; that is
  how paint comes off the canvas.
- **Everything else** the easel does is in the easel guide.

- **Habit.** A straight, regular trunk up to 50–60 m, usually living 200–300 years. "The crown is regularly conic, columnar, with whorled, short and stout branches, the upper level ascending and the lower drooping". Free-standing trees keep green branches down to the ground. Branches are inclined to hanging, as an adaptation to snow load.
- **Branching types.** Young spruces branch in flat "plates" up to about 20 years. After that they develop either the *Plattenfichte* type, with horizontal second-order branches, or the *Kammfichte* ("comb spruce") type, whose second- and higher-order branches hang down like a fringe. A third type is the *Bürstenfichte* ("brush spruce"). Comb spruces dominate on well-supplied sites. Plate spruces dominate on poor bogs and at extreme altitudes.
- **Bark.** Orange-brown. Red-brown and scaly, later gray with flaking scales or plates. Drops of resin are common on trunk and branches.

### 3.8 Scots pine (*Pinus sylvestris*)

- **Habit.** 23–27 m on average, sometimes over 40 m. It lives 400 years or more. Crowns are rounded when young and round-topped when old. The trunk is often twisted, depending on seed origin. In some conifers, flattening and broadening of the crown may be the only sign of old-age retrenchment.
- **Bark.** The upper stem is "a distinct reddish-orange," while the lower part is "furrowed brown to grey-brown and becomes deeply fissured". "Upper crowns always show orange peeling bark".
- **Needles.** In pairs, twisted.

A usable range for 19th-century canvases is **10–38 threads/cm**, which is a **0.26–1.0 mm pitch**. Warp and weft often differ by 10–40%.

- **Irregularity.** Density along the warp is always more consistent than along the weft[V]. Weft "slubs" (thick spots) are the usual irregularity[S].
- **Cusping (scalloping).** This is "a regular scalloping of the threads at the perimeter" left by the tacks used while the canvas was sized and grounded[V]. On the 1879/80 canvas the original tacks were **5.5–6 cm apart**[V]. Commercial pre-primed rolls often show *no* cusping on edges cut from the roll[V].
- **Ground and texture.** Late-19th-century commercial grounds were either *à grain* (one layer, so more weave texture shows) or *lisse* (two layers, fills the interstices)[S]. An **estimate is 5–40 µm** peak to valley under *à grain* and about 2–10 µm under *lisse* **[E, unverified]**.
- **Mechanics.** Above about 80% RH the canvas *shrinks* as crimp increases, and once dry the glue size, not the canvas, carries the tension[V].

events.text:
I'm thinking through the hallmarks of Friedrich's style to capture in an original landscape—the solitary figure gazing outward, misty atmospheric light, and dark detailed silhouettes against luminous skies.

Rather than copying any of his famous works like Wanderer above the Sea of Fog or Monk by the Sea, I want to invent a genuinely new composition that channels the same melancholic, sublime mood. I'm now starting to plan the technical setup for rendering it—a wide oil-on-linen canvas with generous proportions to capture that sense of vastness.

I'm sketching an idea for a dawn scene over a frozen estuary, with a low horizon and thin distant band, drawing on his techniques of smooth sky gradation and glazed brushwork.

I'm weighing other compositions too—a moonrise over a hill with a lone pine and distant mist feels too close to "Wanderer above the Sea of Fog," so I'm drifting toward a quieter idea: a still Baltic coastline at dusk.

More options come up—a ruined chapel on a hill among spruces, or a hilltop view over a misty river plain at dawn with a figure seen from behind—but these all echo existing works too closely. I need something original, so I'm starting to break the composition down into basic elements, beginning with the sky's gradation.

I'm picturing the sky shifting from warm pale yellow-orange near the horizon to cool blue-grey at the top, with thin layered pink-grey clouds, painted smoothly and occupying most of the canvas as Friedrich typically did. Then the middle distance holds bluish, mist-softened hill silhouettes, the foreground carries sharp dark details like a bare oak or spruces, rocks, and grass, and a small dark-coated figure stands with their back to the viewer—while I also need to account for drying time between glazed layers.

I'm now settling on a unifying mood: a quiet, melancholy twilight over a flat tidal flat or lake, sun just set, sky glowing in bands, a gnarled dead oak silhouetted on a rise to the left, and a solitary figure seated on a stone gazing outward—echoing works like "Two Men Contemplating the Moon" or the stark horizontal minimalism of "Monk by the Sea," which would suit the simulator's strengths in smooth gradients and simple shapes while still carrying emotional weight.

I'm also recalling "Cross in the Mountains" with its sunbeam rays and silhouetted spruces for inspiration, but reminding myself the subject should be my own invention—maybe a boat-graveyard on a misty Baltic shore, or dawn over the Elbe meadows with a church tower and poplars. I'm weighing these options to settle on one.

I'm now checking which tools support the technique: brushwork for broad strokes and glazing, stippling, outlining for tree silhouettes, and graphite pencil underdrawing in Friedrich's historical manner, where thin paint layers let the sketch show through. I'm also thinking about his warm, multi-layered grounds.

For the ground I'm sketching a layered preparation—red earth and ochre beneath, lead white on top—applied with a knife then a roller. I'm also mapping brush types to purposes: rigger for fine branches, fan for foliage, badger for blending sky, and planning on thin lean layers that need roughly a day to dry between passes.

Since painting time passes instantly, I can build classical layered work—underpainting, drying, then glazes. For skies I'm thinking band-by-band strokes (warm horizon, pale middle, blue top) blended vertically, treating this as a painted gradation rather than an encoded image, which fits the rule against computing pictures directly.

I'm mapping out a historical palette: lead white, smalt, pale smalt, yellow ochre, red earth, vermilion, raw umber, bone black, cobalt blue, chrome yellow, Prussian blue, green earth, Rinmann's green, copper green. For the sky I'd mix white with warm ochre or vermilion near the horizon and smalt/cobalt higher up, with pink and gray clouds from vermilion and umber-blue mixes, while silhouette trees and darks come from umber, Prussian blue, and bone black combinations.

Now I'm sketching the actual scene, weighing Friedrich-inspired ideas without copying him directly — a lone figure at a cliff's edge overlooking a misty valley at dawn, or a woman in period dress watching the sunrise, or perhaps a shepherd's hut beside a solitary linden tree, trying to find the composition with the right quiet, solemn emotional weight.

Also there's "Moonrise over the Sea" with figures on rocks watching ships arrive — a strong Friedrichian theme. I'm weighing which composition best shows off the simulator: a luminous sky with subtle gradations and thin cloud bands, a low horizon, a finely drawn dark foreground silhouette, and a tiny figure for scale.

I could go coastal — a leafless oak, maybe a dolmen, a lone figure from behind on a stone, with the sea's low horizon line and a thin strip of light — echoing Monk by the Sea or Moonrise. Or alternatively a mountain scene: a dark rock pinnacle in the lower left, a mist-filled valley below with distant ridges, under a wide golden dawn sky.

Mist layers would let me simulate atmospheric perspective nicely, each ridge progressively lighter and bluer — that's classic Friedrich, echoing Wanderer or Morning in the Riesengebirge. I'd soften the gradations with a blender, add dark foreground rocks and a dead spruce or two, and place the Rückenfigur off-center. But this risks feeling too close to Wanderer, so I'm weighing alternatives: two figures instead of one, a view from within a forest clearing, or a hill with a cross as the focal subject.

I'm also considering a ruined chapel on a rocky outcrop at dawn, something like a monastery graveyard in snow, and thinking through which compositional elements I can render most convincingly — simple smooth sky and sea, and spruce silhouettes built from a trunk line with downward-sweeping, tiered stroke clusters mimicking Friedrich's delicate branch work.

Each tree needs its own independently drawn coordinates rather than mirrored or copied shapes, though I can reuse a parametric helper with randomized branch angles to vary each one. For an oak, I'm thinking a recursive branching function with random gnarled angles and decreasing stroke widths to capture its bare, twisting structure.

Now I'm moving to composition, thinking through Friedrich's design principles—horizon placement, whether low or high.

Other key elements: dark repoussoir silhouettes framing the foreground, light pooling at the horizon with warm-to-cool gradient, small spiritual symbols like a cross or ruin, a restrained cool palette punctuated by warm horizon tones, and smooth meticulous sky surfaces. I'm also considering titles like "Evening Beyond the Heath" or "Morning Fog over the Elbe."

A distinctive composition idea occurs to me: a massive bare oak with crooked limbs dominating the left third against a luminous sky, with a three-stone dolmen doorway at its base framing a glowing horizon — though this risks echoing Friedrich's "Hünengrab im Herbst" too directly. I'm also weighing an alternative: a frozen river scene with an upturned boat and lone mast.

Shifting focus to luminosity and feasibility, I'm drawn to a sea-of-fog structure or a low sun glowing behind thin clouds over calm water with a distant sail — maybe something like "Dawn Fog over the Oderbruch." Other Friedrichian possibilities include a mountain pass with a wooden cross and solitary hiker above the clouds, or "The Evening Star" with a lone figure on a plain beneath a star, and I'm starting to sketch out the actual composition proportions and horizon placement for a landscape-format piece.

Thinking through the layout, I picture the sky dominating the upper 60%, a dark headland on the left with spruces and a lone dead pine silhouetted against the glow, and the right side opening onto a misty sea or valley with receding ridges. A Rückenfigur — one or two dark-coated figures with a staff — stands near a cairn on the headland, gazing into a hidden sun's warm glow breaking through the cloud bank.

I'm weighing whether to make this a sunrise or sunset scene versus a moonlit "Mondaufgang" mood instead, since Friedrich's work often shifts between warm horizon glows and cool blue-green nocturnes with a pale lunar disc and soft stars.

Rather than echoing the famous Chalk Cliffs composition, I think I'll create something original in his spirit—a misty valley with receding ridges at twilight, giving me flexibility for subtle atmospheric gradients while still feeling distinctly mine rather than a direct copy.

I want to build on restrained value shapes readable from far away with finer details for close inspection, checking the composition in squint and value modes. I'm sketching an idea of a Rückenfigur on a dune beside dead pines, facing a calm sea toward a distant sailing ship under a vast luminous sky with layered clouds, though dunes feel slightly off from Friedrich's usual terrain despite Monk by the Sea.

I'm weighing a mountain-valley-fog scene with light coming from behind the viewer, or a twilight Elbe valley with a solitary figure on a hillside, and thinking practically about pacing — planning roughly 40-80 tool-call chunks to carefully build sky, distant fog, mid-ground forms, foreground silhouettes, and fine details, starting with some test strokes to get familiar with the tools before committing.

Since there's no separate test canvas and every stroke stays permanently on the single painting, I realize experiments need to happen somewhere they'll later be hidden — the smartest spot is the lower foreground area, which I'll eventually cover with opaque dark silhouette paint, letting me safely test how each tool behaves before painting it over.

Now I'm sizing the canvas: thinking through mm dimensions matching Friedrich's typical scale (around 900mm wide with a 1.3 aspect ratio), and working out how thread count per cm translates to pixel density across a 2400px canvas, considering finer linen weaves like 16x15 threads for the right texture.

At 1 unit ≈ 2.4 px, a 0.5-unit rigger would render about 1.2 px wide, which seems workable even for small figures around 48 px tall. Thinking of Friedrich's actual dimensions—"Monk by the Sea" and "Wanderer above the Sea of Fog"—I'll settle on a canvas size that mirrors those proportions.

I'll pick 1000mm as the width so 1 unit equals 1mm, keeping the math simple. For aspect ratio, something around 1.3-1.35 feels right to emphasize horizontal vastness without going too wide for the pixel budget—landscape orientation suits the sky-heavy composition better than portrait. Now I'm thinking through the ground layers: a warm reddish-ochre base transitioning to lighter tones higher up, echoing Friedrich's typical palette structure.

For the grounding technique, I'm leaning toward a warm earth-and-ochre base applied with a knife for texture, topped with a lighter white-ochre layer brushed on to create subtle striations that will show through thinner paint later. I'm unsure whether I can call canvas setup more than once or preview the ground before committing to paint—I may just need to set it up, check the result, and adjust from there if needed.

Now turning to the real artistic question: composition. I'm brainstorming several Friedrich-style scene ideas—a flat heath with an ancient burial mound and a single dead oak, a misty sea view, a shipwreck on the Baltic shore at dawn—weighing which captures that melancholic Romantic sensibility best before committing to one.

Meadows near a river at dawn, mist rising with sunlight reflecting in shallow pools, poplars and willows as vertical accents, maybe a small fisherman's boat on the water—though the reflections would need careful soft handling. I jot down a few more fleeting ideas too: a seated figure with a dog overlooking a glowing distant city at dusk, and a mountain hut scene.

Now I'm weighing a dramatic alternative—a lone dead spruce on a rocky outcrop with a wanderer seen from behind facing a glowing sea between two ridges, echoing "The Wanderer." Comparing this against the shipwreck idea, I find the wreck more compelling: its skeletal hull ribs make a striking foreground silhouette against a vast, calm low-tide seascape with wet sand reflecting sunset light, distant sails, a far shore with a tiny chapel, a thin crescent moon, and perhaps a small solitary figure.

I'm thinking through how to paint the wet sand reflection—essentially a soft, hand-painted gradient mirroring the sky's color in horizontal bands rather than literally flipping any shapes. This wreck-on-tidal-flat concept still fits squarely within Friedrich's Baltic visual vocabulary of solitary figures, mist, and quiet desolation.

Now I'm weighing whether to add more elements like a dune, windblown pine, or Rückenfigur figure, but I'm leaning toward restraint—Monk by the Sea works because it's sparse: tiny figure, vast subtle sky, twilight mood. I'm considering inventing a stand-in figure rather than a literal monk to keep that same spare power.

Actually, thinking about what excites me most as the artist, I keep returning to the fog-filled valley with layered ridges fading into mist, spruce silhouettes, and a lone figure—this is quintessentially Friedrich territory, echoing works like "Wanderer above the Sea of Fog" and "Der Watzmann." The interplay of ridge silhouettes through atmospheric haze feels like both a beautiful image and a genuine test of how well the rendering can capture subtle tonal gradation.

I'm working out the layered composition: near dark ridge, mist bands, a paler mid-ridge, then a distant glowing horizon with the sun half-hidden, all under a classic Friedrich stratus sky. For the Rückenfigur, I'm picturing a lone man in a dark-green coat and hat, like a hunter, standing with his back to the viewer.

I keep debating the figure's exact styling, maybe a dark red dress and bonnet instead, but settling on a dark silhouette standing on the foreground rock, one hand on a staff, readable as head, shoulders, and a flaring coat. I'm sketching through how a small round brush could render that silhouette convincingly at the scale this canvas allows.

Now I'm working out the canvas proportions, leaning toward a wide aspect around 1.3 to give the sky room, and thinking through Friedrich-style compositions like Wanderer and Morning Mist in the Mountains as models for asymmetric balance—settling on a plan with a rock promontory rising from the bottom-left as the foreground anchor.

I'm sketching the rest of the scene: the figure standing near the top of that promontory, a counterbalancing cluster of three spruces (one dead) on a lower spur to the right, and layered ridge silhouettes in the mid-ground. This feels close to a mashup of Wanderer and Cross in the Mountains though, so I want to push for something more distinctive while still staying true to Friedrich's sensibility, considering alternate scenarios like a pilgrim's ford or river crossing.

Another option forming: a path through snow-laden spruces at winter dusk leading to a fogbound gothic ruin under moonlight. I'm also weighing "The Evening Boat" — a rowboat with two figures crossing a still twilight river toward a silhouetted town, its glow reflected on glassy water, framed by dark reeds and bare willow stumps in the foreground, echoing Friedrich's dusk river scenes.

I'm weighing options against criteria: fidelity to Friedrich's style, feasibility at high quality, distinctiveness, and emotional resonance — comparing the mountain-fog scene, the river-dusk scene, and a shipwreck idea, while also considering something closer to "Sea of Ice" territory, though that feels too complex. I keep returning to Friedrich's signature elements: a solitary figure seen from behind, a luminous sky, a silhouetted dead tree, and drifting mist.

I'm now settling on a composition — a hilltop at dawn overlooking a fog-filled plain, a distant town's spires emerging through the haze, a pale sun breaking the horizon, and in the foreground a massive bare oak with branches tracing across the glowing sky, alongside a seated figure with a hound viewed from behind. This feels like a strong, distinctly Friedrich-like scene.

Though I'm reconsidering — maybe it's too crowded with the oak, figure, dog, fog, town, and sun all at once. Friedrich's work tends toward sparseness, so I might cut the dog and the town, keeping just the oak, the figure, and the glowing fog valley with a hint of a distant ridge or spire. I'm thinking through the backlighting: the low sun behind the fog would silhouette the foreground elements in dark, warm-rimmed shapes while the sky and fog glow pale gold.

I'm also weighing a dawn setting versus a twilight blue-hour version, since the dusk palette with its warm horizon band fading through a greenish-turquoise transition into deep blue above feels like a richer, more Friedrich-esque color harmony against the dark foreground silhouette.

Now I'm mapping out the actual sky palette — warm pale gold near the horizon, a greenish transition built from thin overlapping layers of yellow and blue, then a cooler blue-gray higher up, with warmer tones reserved for the cloud bands.

I'm also thinking through the composition's value structure: dark foreground elements like the oak and figure, mid-value ridges, and a bright sky with the horizon as the brightest point. Then I'm working out the geometry — placing a Rückenfigur near the left-center edge with coat and hat, and comparing horizon placement to Friedrich's "Wanderer" and "Monk by the Sea" to decide roughly where it should sit on a 1000×769 canvas.

For the oak, I sketch options: a massive tree filling the left half with crown and branches spreading wide like in "Abbey in the Oakwood," or a smaller, cropped tree at the left edge with the figure positioned on the knoll beside it, leaving the right side open.

I favor asymmetry — tree on the left, open misty view on the right, with the horizon glow placed center-right. For the branches themselves, I want gnarled, twisting limbs with irregular widths and sinuous curves, some broken or dead, rendered as smooth paths with angular noise and widths that taper following natural branching rules.

Thinking through the painting process itself like Friedrich would: start with a warm ground, then a light graphite underdrawing of horizon, ridges, and trunk placement that will subtly show through thin paint layers, followed by thin imprimatura-style underpainting of sky and ridges built up in dried layers before glazing in gradations and clouds.

For the mist, foreground darks, and final detail passes, I'm thinking through how the simulator's blending tools work -- using a glaze hand over a masked area with a pile, then blending with crossing passes to create smooth, stroke-free gradients like Friedrich's skies, possibly building the gradient from horizontal bands of color blended top to bottom with a badger brush.

For horizontal bands I'd use horizontal strokes with a wide badger, keeping in mind that lead-white-rich paint stays open for about two hours and large passes take real time to lay down, so early strokes may start setting before later ones are applied. I'm considering adding medium to slow drying and keep the sky workable during blending, though too much would make the paint too transparent.

I'm also weighing an alternative of thin glazing layers built up over several dried passes, each with gentle graded loads based on vertical position, echoing Friedrich's technique of very thin layers. A gradient load varying with height risks brushing against the rule against encoding an image as a function of coordinates, though a smooth tonal gradient feels like a legitimate painterly gesture rather than computed imagery -- still, I'd rather lean primarily on physical technique to stay safely within that boundary.

So I'm settling on painting horizontal bands of varying color and wet-blending them, using the load function only sparingly for smoothing, since the blender can only move wet paint and not set or dry layers. For clouds I'm planning thin stratus bands with soft edges glazed over dry sky, scumbled pinkish-white tones blended gently; for the distant ridges I'm thinking of hand-drawn masks with softened outlines filled with bluish paint, with a pale misty band at the base.

Then there's the glaze dissolving into the ridge, the foreground hill rendered in dark umber-green with grass strokes and rocks, and I want to check the composition using squint and value modes to catch structural issues before committing. I'm wary of the simulation producing uneven or overly strong textures, so I'll build things up gradually and test as I go. For the underdrawing, I'm working out the canvas proportions, leaning toward a wider aspect ratio around 1.35 to give the sky and fog valley room to breathe alongside a large foreground oak on the left.

I settle on a landscape aspect of 1.25, giving a 1000×800 canvas (2400×1920 px full resolution, scaled to 1600×1280 for viewing), rejecting a portrait orientation since the horizontal fog sea is the stronger compositional driver. Then I return to refining the core concept: a solitary figure atop a hill at first light, a sea of fog below, and an ancient half-dead oak beside them symbolizing endurance and transience at once.

I decide the oak should be stag-headed, with dead upper limbs rising above a still-living lower crown, its masses uneven rather than one tidy dome — closer to Friedrich's bare winter oaks than a leafy autumn tree, since foliage would add unwanted complexity and dilute the cool, stark mood I want against the fog.

For the figure, I'm leaning away from the standard wanderer toward a solitary person seen from behind, perhaps a woman in a dark red-brown dress and white cap echoing Friedrich's "Woman before the Setting Sun," since a small warm accent of color against an otherwise cool composition would be striking. I'm also weighing a man in a long dark coat with a staff and auburn hair as an alternative, to introduce that same touch of warmth without overdoing it.

I want to avoid simply recreating "Wanderer" too closely, so I'm reconsidering the composition: placing the viewer slightly behind and below the figure, maybe with the figure off-center, and introducing a winding footpath that passes the oak and leads diagonally up to the figure at the crest, using the path itself as a compositional device to guide the eye.

Actually, I think the stronger focal point could be the sunrise itself—a pale molten sun disc just breaking over a distant ridge, its glow turning the mist golden and casting a luminous path across the fog layers, with the figure's gaze drawn toward that light against the darker foreground.

I'm happy with the composition now, though I'm considering small touches like a thin silver ribbon of river winding through the fog valley, or perhaps a tiny church spire poking subtly above the mist for a Friedrich-like touch of human presence.

For the mist itself, I want soft-edged lighter bands over the ridge silhouettes, blending warm tones near the sun into cooler blue further out, with lost edges blended with a badger brush. Given the scale of this project, I'm breaking it into chunks: canvas prep, ground layer, then underdrawing the horizon and ridges.

Continuing the underdrawing with the oak trunk and limbs, the figure, and the hill line, then checking the result before laying in a thin sky underpainting and letting it dry. I need to remember that thin paint over a pale ground reads lighter, warmer, and more saturated than its full-strength mass tone, so I'll need to compensate for that when mixing. To avoid wet-into-wet problems, I'll paint sky first, then ridges progressing from far to near, then the foreground, letting each layer partially overlap for soft transitions.

For the oak silhouette and branches, I'll paint them opaque over the fully dry sky with a fine rigger brush, keeping edges crisp, and letting the finest twig tips go lighter and softer to suggest atmosphere. Since the oak sits close on the hill, it reads strongly dark and silhouetted against the cooler, mid-value sky above the horizon, giving moderate but effective contrast — even though the fine branchwork will take many small strokes, that's worth the time for the detail it adds.

For the foreground ground plane, I'll add small blade-textured grass near the figure and a few edge-lit boulder shapes for interest. For the mid-ground, I'm considering a lower ridge lined with small dark spruce silhouettes — tiny conical spikes of varying heights along the crest, painted with a pointed round brush, evoking that Friedrich "Morning in the Riesengebirge" look of evergreen spires rising through fog.

Writing ridge mask code...

I'm planning the composition at 1000x800: placing the sun's glow just above the farthest horizon around x=660, y=470, then sketching the faintest distant ridge as a gentle hand-placed point-list curve that rises and dips across the width before forming soft mountain peaks toward the right edge.

Now I'm figuring out the fog layer spanning the full width around y=480–560, with mid and near ridges poking through like islands—R2 with spruce silhouettes, and R1 forming the hilltop where the figure stands, sloping down from the left into the mist.

The hilltop line I'm plotting runs diagonally from the figure's position down to the lower right, creating a strong compositional slope against the fog, with an oak tree anchored at the crest just left of the figure, its trunk cropping at the hill's edge and crown spreading wide above.

I'm repositioning the figure so it's silhouetted against the bright fog band rather than a dark background—placing it slightly right of the oak, standing on a small rise, with head and shoulders catching the glow of the mist behind it, keeping the proportions grounded rather than oversized like the classic Wanderer composition.

Now I'm sizing the oak against the figure: trunk base around 50 units, trunk height to first limbs ~90, crown ~330 — a massive old tree. Using realistic human-to-oak proportions puts the full tree around 640 units tall, which overshoots the canvas, so I need to scale things down or crop the tree into the frame.

Given that, I'm thinking about perspective: if the oak sits closer to the viewer than the figure, it will loom much larger while the figure appears small, echoing Friedrich's compositions where tiny monks stand near towering ruins or trees. So I'll place the oak in the foreground, cropped near the top of the canvas, with the figure positioned farther back along the ridge crest, making the distance difference account for their relative scale.

To avoid it reading as a generic fractal tree, I want sinuous twisting main limbs, irregular mass with lower limbs sweeping and drooping while upper ones turn upward, tapered widths following natural proportions, twig clusters at the tips, and some broken stubs for weathered character.

I'm planning the trunk texture with fissured bark strokes and a lighter rim catching the dawn glow, plus defining the crown silhouette as a few separate masses rather than a uniform ellipse. I'll hand-place the main limbs as weighted polylines and let finer branches generate procedurally from them, rendering each stroke with a pointed brush whose width responds to pressure like a real rigger brush.

For taper, each branch stroke runs from high pressure at the base to near-zero at the tip, giving a natural point. For thicker limbs I'm considering ribbon masks with varying widths along each limb's path, filled crisply with clipping, then unioning many mid-size limb ribbons into one mask I can paint at once with a dark pile following the limb direction — though I still need to work out how stroke orientation should follow the branch direction.

For branches I'd generate the polyline as a gentle random walk with persistent direction, then feed that into the stroke so it smooths naturally, with a rigger/round brush for the finer hairline tips. The trunk would use a wider flat/filbert brush painted along its length, or masked work calls for thicker coverage. Since everything runs as Lua inside a paint chunk, I can define reusable helper functions globally, and it's reassuring that errored chunks leave no changes, which makes experimentation safe.

For actual testing, though, a chunk that executes without error but looks ugly will still stick, so I should confine early trials to areas that will later be covered by darker foreground paint — testing glaze-hand work for pale mid-tones on the ground, testing blend, and checking how visible a pencil underdrawing stays beneath thin paint. Thinking Friedrich-style, the underdrawing should really come first: sketching the horizon, ridgelines, hill crest, and the oak's major limbs before anything else.

Now I'm working out the drawing itself — using light 2H pressure for the figure, rocks, and tree lines, relying on sketch, line, and rule tools for thin passes. Since graphite resists wet paint and gets sealed once painted over, thin paint will let the lines show while opaque color hides them.

For the ground color, a pale warm base would let the sky glow through thin paint, while thin dark mixtures laid over that same pale ground would come out lighter, warmer, and more saturated than a straight masstone — so for the darker foreground I'll likely need thicker, more opaque paint or multiple layers, possibly starting with a thin warm-brown imprimatura to establish depth before building up the darks.

I'm settling on a two-layer ground: a warm reddish-ocher base beneath a lighter, lead-white-rich top layer, mixing specific ratios of red earth, yellow ochre, lead white, and raw umber applied with knife and brush at different thicknesses. I'll test this by generating a blank canvas and visually checking the ground tone, with the option to redo it if it doesn't look right.

I'm also deciding on practical setup details — picking an arbitrary seed, a linen thread count around 15x14, and a canvas scale of 1 unit per millimeter, which seems to pair sensibly with the default brush sizes (a 9mm "body" brush and 22mm "broad" brush matching real filbert brush proportions).

I could use roller for a finely textured structure, but brush striations showing faintly through thin sky glazes feels more historically apt for the top layer—though too much texture risks looking brushy. I'll test brush first and see how it reads.
I'll set up the canvas first.

events.name: paint

events.text: I notice the ground has a warm cream tone. Since the image is scaled down from a larger 2400px version, I want to check a 1:1 crop to examine the texture more closely.

The ground looks smooth and warm, cream-colored with faint brush texture, reminiscent of a Friedrich ground. I note that warm glazes will glow through nicely, though cool sky blues might turn slightly greenish-gray against it—which actually matches Friedrich's characteristic sky tones anyway.

Now I'm moving to underdrawing, planning the main structural lines in graphite: horizon and ridge lines, foreground crest, tree limbs, figure, and rocks. I'm working out the composition geometry on a 1000x800 canvas, placing the sun low near the farthest ridge around y≈470, deciding to make it a soft, diffused, creamy disc rather than a hard-edged one—like a low dawn sun seen through haze.

I'm layering the horizon from far to near: a distant mountain range and ridge, a mid-far pale ridge, nearer wooded hills emerging from fog, a fog band filling the valley with the glow, and finally the foreground crest sloping down from the oak at left to a dark lower-right slope where the figure stands partway along it.

Rather than leaving the lower right as plain dark, I'm thinking of giving it more interest—maybe a second dark spur with silhouetted spruces rising into the fog glow on the right, mirroring the oak and forming a V-shaped valley open to the misty sea, like theatrical wings framing the scene in a Friedrich/Lorrain style.

For the figure, I'm placing him at the left crest near the edge, looking outward, standing just beneath the oak's right-reaching limbs so the canopy arches over him without truly overlapping—since he's farther back in the perspective, the gap under the branches naturally frames him.

Thinking through the ground logic now: the oak sits nearer on the foreground slope with its base lower on the canvas, while the figure stands higher up at the crest, so I need to work out how the hill's rise toward the valley view affects their relative positions.

The hill's silhouette dips lower on the right, meaning the viewer stands near a diagonal edge of the hill. I'm placing a dark foreground band covering roughly 28% of the image with the oak on the left, and a rock outcrop near (365, 538) where the figure stands, with a lighter footpath winding through dry grass and stones toward it. Now I'm ready to sketch the oak's skeleton before procedurally adding detail.

I'm mapping out the trunk's base and lean, then tracing how it forks into three or four massive limbs about a third of the way up, plotting rough coordinates and widths for each branch as they curve and taper outward.

Continuing to plot the limbs, including one stretching rightward across the sky above the figure's head, a drooping lower-left branch that may run off the canvas edge, and extra crossing branches for a fuller, more tangled oak silhouette.

I'm designing the crown to look asymmetrical and stag-headed, with bare gray-silver limbs at top and denser twig mass lower down. Writing branching generator code...

I'm exploring brush parameters like stiffness, splay, and bristles to test stroke widths, and considering using a body_of/outline function that builds a silhouette mask from a skeleton of points and widths — perfect for painting the oak's organic trunk and main limbs.

For finer branches I'll use stroke-based work with clipping to keep edges crisp, layering lighter and darker bark texture strokes inside the mask. I'm thinking about a Friedrich-style flat silhouette with just a touch of warm rim light on the right-facing edges of the trunk and limbs for subtle depth, and debating whether to leave the crown bare or add sparse clusters of dried brownish leaves for texture.

I'll keep the oak mostly bare apart from a few silvery dead branches. Before painting I want to lay down a basic underdrawing—horizon, ridges, crest, figure, trunk and main limbs—and I'm realizing it makes sense to define the tree's limb skeleton once and reuse it both as a light pencil sketch and as the structural basis for the painted mask, so the drawing functions as a real plan rather than a throwaway sketch.

Since the graphite lines will show faintly through thin glazes where not covered by dark paint, I should only pencil in the main limbs that will actually be painted over, skipping fine branch tips that might extend past their final painted shape and read as stray marks. I'm weighing whether a full light pencil pass over everything is worth it versus just the landscape lines, since letting horizon and ridge lines subtly show through the misty layers could give that crisp, Friedrich-like quality.

I'm now working out the placement of the distant mountain ridges, plotting their rise and fall as a polyline and deciding where they should peak relative to the sun's position so they don't compete with the oak tree's silhouette.

I'm placing two darker hill humps emerging from the fog, with spruce spikes along their tops, since they sit in front of R3. I'm working out that the fog level sits between the far horizon and the hilltop viewpoint, so the fog reads as a bright flat plane with these hills poking up above its surface like islands.

That might overbalance the composition toward light at bottom-right, mirroring the dark mass at bottom-left into a strong diagonal split like Wanderer's value structure. I'm considering adding a dark feature there, like a rocky spruce-covered spur or a lone silhouetted tree rising from the fog, to avoid leaving the corner as plain gradient and to reconsider the crest line's geometry for balance.

Actually, horizontal layering might read stronger than a diagonal — bottom ground, fog band, ridges, then sky dominating, echoing something like "Monk by the Sea," with the oak anchoring the left and scattered spruce silhouettes along the crest's edge. I'll settle on the crest descending gently from left to right, roughly y=535 down toward y=600.

Scaling the elements so the massive oak on the left dwarfs the smaller mid-size spruce cluster on the right, with the figure, sun glow, and fog filling the center and the sky dominating overall feels right.

For the fog, I want it to grade from warm cream-gold near the sun down to cooler bluish-lavender and shadowed gray-blue near the foreground crest, adding atmospheric depth. For the sky, I'm planning three cloud layers above a cool blue-gray upper sky and warm horizon glow -- starting with a band of long horizontal strata clouds catching pink light.

Below that I'll add wispy pale cirrus streaking diagonally higher up, then a low thin haze at the horizon, keeping things sparse and clear the way Friedrich's foggy-morning skies tend to be. The sun itself stays a pale, hazy disc with nearby strata glowing orange-pink, and I'm considering adding a few faint crepuscular rays fanning upward as subtle lighter wedges for that spiritual-light effect.

Now I'm sketching the standing Rückenfigur, working out his proportions and placement—feet near the bottom, head at a fixed height, shoulder width, coat silhouette widening toward the hem, and a thin staff held in his hand—sized to be noticeable but not dominate the composition. I'm mapping out the initial pencil underdrawing lines for the distant ridges.

Next I'm planning the remaining underdrawing: the crest line, the rock beneath the figure, the figure's outline, the oak's trunk and main limbs, and the spruce shapes at the right rendered as simple cones. Then I'm considering how this light 2H pencil work should remain faintly visible beneath the thin mist glazes over the ridges, and working out how to code the sketching passes with light pressure and slight hand-wander rather than a rigid ruled line.

Now I'm plotting the ridge coordinates layer by layer, starting with the farthest mountain silhouette on the right and the long low ridge in front of it, thinking through how the nearer ridge should read darker and more saturated while partially overlapping the base of the farther one.

Next I'm placing the two mid-ground humps, A and B, checking whether they sit too close together and considering how the figure standing near x=360 interacts visually with hump A's rising slope and head height.

To keep the figure's silhouette readable against bright fog rather than blending into the hump, I'm shifting hump A further left so it ends before x=330, moving the figure to around x=392, and placing hump B further right with its crest near x=545, leaving the sun glow region between them bright behind the figure.

I'm also mapping out the near crest line, which descends gradually from around y=545 near the left edge to y=672 by x=1000, giving the terrain a consistent rightward slope toward distant fog.

I'm reconsidering a spruce group near the right edge — if placed around x 840-960, it would obscure the far mountain peaks there, so I'm thinking of shifting it further right to x 920-990, partially cropped off-canvas, so the distant peaks stay visible to its left. I'm also weighing leaving that side open entirely, letting the eye travel toward the sun and far mountains instead.

A modest trio of spruces, heights 140-230, rising from y≈660 to tips around y 430-520 and cropped at the frame edge, would give the right side just enough counterweight to the oak without competing as a second focal tree. Since they sit a touch farther back on the hill crest, I'll paint them slightly less dark and a bit bluer than the oak to keep the depth reading correct.

I'm also considering a foreground anchor at the bottom — maybe a dark, partially cropped boulder with grass tufts at the bottom-right corner, or a rock slab at bottom center, to be judged once the overall composition is in place. For the underdrawing I'm now setting up the oak's structural skeleton as a data table capturing the trunk spine points and widths plus the limb definitions, so I can reuse this geometry consistently when building out the branches.

Since the final painted mass will cover the pencil lines in the trunk and limb areas, I want the pencil guide to match the actual limb positions so only the branch tips peeking past the foliage stay visible — meaning I should build the skeleton once and share it between the underdrawing and the final paint pass. Now I'm roughing out the trunk's base dimensions, including the root flare near the ground.

Adding first main limb coordinates...

Now mapping the other primary limbs: a center-high limb rising with slight bends, a right "reaching" limb curving gently toward the light and dominating the crown's right side, and a lower-left drooping limb sketched in toward the left edge.

I'm deciding to skip a lower-right drooping limb since it would intersect awkwardly with the figure and the hills below, keeping only the lower-left droop. I still need to add secondary branches off these main limbs and some dead, stag-head branches near the top-left.

For color, I'm planning a cool dark brown-black with a slight green-blue shift for the oak's silhouette, with faint warm-gray highlights catching the upper surfaces of the limbs, since the tree's crown is cropped by the top and left edges to suggest its massive size. Now I'm starting the underdrawing code that builds the trunk and limb silhouette before layering in twig-level strokes.

Writing the pencil setup and mountain ridge points...

Now I'm sketching out the oak tree's structure, defining trunk points with tapering width and branching limb coordinates.

Now I'm sketching the figure's proportions from behind—head, neck, and shoulder width scaled relative to overall height, using realistic human proportion ratios to position the coat and shoulders correctly.

I'm plotting silhouette points down each side of the body—head, neck, shoulder, arm, hip, hem—keeping the sides slightly asymmetrical to suggest a natural pose, and adding a staff planted at the figure's left side extending from shoulder height down to the ground.

For the staff, I'll keep it taller than the figure, sketched lightly in pencil since dark paint will cover most of it later. Then I'll loosely place three spruce trees at the right with simple trunk lines and base-width ticks, saving the jagged cone details for paint, while skipping any pencil marks for the sun or horizon.
